concept.name: Stochastic volatility model
concept.definition: A class of models in which volatility is itself a latent stochastic process evolving with its own innovations, rather than a deterministic function of past observed shocks as in GARCH. In continuous time, Heston (1993) models variance as a mean-reverting square-root process driven by its own Brownian motion, possibly correlated with the price shock.
concept.intuition: Volatility is an unobserved state variable that wanders randomly and mean-reverts; you see it only through the size of price moves, so inference filters the hidden volatility out of the return data.
concept.mechanics: In the Heston specification, dS_t = mu S_t dt + sqrt(v_t) S_t dW^S_t and dv_t = kappa (theta - v_t) dt + sigma_v sqrt(v_t) dW^v_t with correlation rho between the Brownian motions; rho < 0 generates the leverage effect and the implied-volatility skew. Estimation uses filtering or method-of-moments for discrete SV, or semi-closed-form characteristic functions for option pricing under Heston.
concept.formula: dv_t = kappa (theta - v_t) dt + sigma_v sqrt(v_t) dW^v_t, corr(dW^S_t, dW^v_t) = rho; kappa is the mean-reversion speed, theta the long-run variance, and sigma_v the vol-of-vol.
concept.failure_modes: The latent state makes the likelihood intractable in closed form, so estimation is computationally heavy and mean-reversion and vol-of-vol parameters are weakly identified on short samples. Wrong volatility dynamics misprice options even when returns are fit well.
concept.misconceptions: That stochastic volatility and GARCH are interchangeable: GARCH variance is measurable given past data, whereas SV variance has its own shock, an extra source of randomness with different option-pricing implications.
concept.example: Heston's semi-closed-form option formula uses the characteristic function of the stock under stochastic variance, reproducing the volatility smile that constant-variance Black-Scholes cannot.
